notes: Ruling slot 0 = UNC (Ahidjo), coalition slot 13 = the presidential technocracy under Paul Biya (Secretary-General of the Presidency since 1968). The former West Cameroon parties (KNDP, CPNC) and the pre-1966 southern parties (PDC, PSC) are all formally dissolved into or suppressed by the UNC by 1970; they are kept as the surviving networks of their leaders. UPC split into party/exile leadership (4) and the ALNK maquis (19). Shia slots use the small Lebanese trading community of Douala.

0.name: Union nationale camerounaise
0.text:
The Cameroonian National Union was born on 1 September 1966 when President Ahmadou Ahidjo folded his Union camerounaise and the three West Cameroon parties, the KNDP, CPNC and CUC, into one national organization. Since then it has been the only lawful party of the Federal Republic, and Ahidjo is both its national president and head of state.

The UNC preaches national unity above tribe, region and language, and 'planned liberalism' in the economy: private and French capital guided by five-year plans. It is firmly anchored to France through defence and monetary agreements and treats the UPC insurgency as a communist threat. Its strength lies in Ahidjo's alliance of northern Fulbe notables and southern administrators, and in total control of patronage, the press and the prefectures.

1.name: Parti des démocrates camerounais
1.text:
The Cameroonian Democrats' Party was founded in 1958 by André-Marie Mbida, the territory's first prime minister, after his fall from power. Jailed in 1962 with the other leaders of the Front national unifié, Mbida came out in 1965 nearly blind and broken in health; he has kept out of the single party, and the PDC lives on only as a loyal network among Catholic notables.

The PDC stands for Catholic social teaching, a multiparty constitution and the rule of law, firmly in the Western camp but hostile to Ahidjo's police state. Its base is the Catholic Beti and Eton cocoa country of the Nyong-et-Sanaga, where mission parishes, catechists and planters' cooperatives still remember Mbida as their own.

2.name: Cameroon People's National Convention
2.text:
The Cameroon People's National Convention was formed in 1960 when Emmanuel Endeley's Kamerun National Congress merged with N. N. Mbile's Kamerun People's Party. It was the opposition in the West Cameroon House of Assembly until 1966, when it was dissolved into the Cameroonian National Union. Endeley and Mbile now sit inside the single party, but the old CPNC network along the coast remains intact.

Its people stand for parliamentary procedure, English common law, free enterprise and an open door to British and Commonwealth investment. The base is the coastal Bakweri and Balong country around Buea, Victoria and Kumba, the plantation economy of the Cameroon Development Corporation, and anglophone lawyers, teachers and traders who distrust both Yaoundé's centralism and the old KNDP machine.

3.name: Parti socialiste camerounais
3.text:
The Socialist Party of Cameroon was founded in November 1959 by Charles Okala, a former senator in Paris, and joined Ahidjo's first government, Okala serving as foreign minister. Arrested in 1962 with the other leaders of the Front national unifié, Okala was released in 1965 on condition that the PSC be dissolved, and its remnants entered the UNC in 1966. Today it survives as a circle of his followers in Yaoundé.

The PSC's tradition is French-style democratic socialism: pluralism, free trade unions, public education and gradual social reform within close ties to France and the West. Its supporters are civil servants, teachers and clerks of the Centre-South who want a socialist voice without the UPC's armed struggle.

4.name: Union des populations du Cameroun
4.english: Union of the Peoples of Cameroon
4.text:
The Union of the Peoples of Cameroon was founded in Douala in April 1948 under Ruben Um Nyobè and banned by the French in 1955. Um Nyobè was killed in 1958 and Félix-Roland Moumié poisoned in Geneva in 1960; the party has since been led inside the country by its vice-president Ernest Ouandié, while exile committees work from Algiers and Brazzaville.

The UPC demands the 'real independence' it says Ahidjo betrayed: the withdrawal of French troops and advisers, an end to the colonial economic system, land reform and a socialist state. It looks to the Soviet bloc, China, Cuba and radical Africa for arms and training. Its roots lie among the Bassa, the Bamiléké and the Mungo, and among Douala dockers, though years of repression have thinned them.
4.wiki: Union of the Peoples of Cameroon

5.name: Union nationale des étudiants du Kamerun
5.native_full: Union nationale des étudiants du Kamerun
5.text:
The National Union of Kamerun Students organizes Cameroonian students in France and is a member of the Federation of Black African Students in France (FEANF). Its very spelling, 'Kamerun', signals its loyalty to the UPC tradition, and Yaoundé treats it as a front of the outlawed party; members returning home risk losing their scholarships or their freedom.

Shaped by the Algerian war, the Vietnam protests and the Paris upheaval of May 1968, UNEK's congresses denounce neocolonialism, French bases and the Ahidjo dictatorship, and debate Maoist and Guevarist roads to revolution. It has no mass base at home, but it trains the future cadres of the opposition and keeps the UPC's cause alive in Paris, Moscow and Beijing.

6.name: Ngondo
6.text:
The Ngondo is the traditional assembly of the Duala and the coastal Sawa peoples, presided over by their paramount chiefs. Revived in the 1940s, it sent petitions to the United Nations against French land seizures and became a voice of early nationalism; it is tolerated today as a cultural body but watched closely by the security services.

The Ngondo defends ancestral land rights in Douala against expropriation by the state and by foreign companies, and guards customs, rites and the memory of King Rudolf Duala Manga Bell, hanged by the Germans in 1914. Its notables resent rule by a northern-dominated regime and its French patrons. Its leverage is the prestige of the old Duala dynasties in the country's largest port city.

7.name: Service des études et de la documentation
7.native_full: Service des études et de la documentation
7.text:
The Studies and Documentation Service is Cameroon's political police, run since the mid-1960s by Jean Fochivé, the most feared official in the country. Together with the paramilitary Brigade mixte mobile and the detention camps of Tcholliré and Mantoum, it is the instrument with which Ahidjo has broken the UPC and silenced every rival.

SEDOC answers to the president alone. Its officers trust neither parliament nor parties, and keep files on ministers, bishops and foreign residents, French advisers included. They favour permanent emergency rule, informer networks in every quarter and an ever larger security budget. Its leverage is fear: few careers in Yaoundé survive an unfavourable SEDOC report.

8.name: Amicale chiite libanaise du Littoral
8.english: Lebanese Shia Friendly Society of the Littoral
8.text:
The Lebanese Shia Friendly Society brings together the families from Jabal Amil in southern Lebanon who trade in cloth, hardware, transport and produce in Douala, Yaoundé and Nkongsamba. Small but prosperous, the community follows events at home closely, above all the rise of Imam Musa al-Sadr, chairman of the new Supreme Islamic Shia Council since 1969.

In Sadr's spirit the society favours education, charity and dialogue with other faiths, and a modern, socially engaged Shiism rather than clerical seclusion. In Cameroon it keeps strictly out of politics and loyal to Ahidjo, relying on discreet contacts with officials. Its influence rests on credit, import licences and the remittances that bind Douala's shops to the villages of south Lebanon.

9.name: Halqat al-Najaf
9.text:
The Najaf Circle is a small study group of devout young Lebanese Shia in Douala who meet around a visiting preacher trained in the seminaries of Najaf. They follow the senior marja Muhsin al-Hakim and listen with interest to the exiled Iranian cleric Ruhollah Khomeini, who teaches in Najaf.

The circle rejects the easy-going secularism of the merchant community and Musa al-Sadr's ecumenism alike, insisting on strict observance, religious dues paid to the marja and the authority of the learned jurist. It is hostile to Israel, the Shah and the Western powers. Its influence is tiny, limited to a handful of households, but it brings the debates of the Najaf hawza to the Cameroonian coast.

10.name: Lamidats du Nord-Cameroun
10.text:
The Lamidates of North Cameroon are the Fulbe Muslim principalities founded in the jihad of the nineteenth century: Garoua, Maroua, Ngaoundéré, Rey Bouba and their many dependencies. Their lamibé still dispense justice, collect tribute and command the loyalty of peasants and clients, and they form the political backbone of President Ahidjo, himself a Fulbe from Garoua.

The lamibé stand for an Islamic social order guided by Maliki law and the Sufi brotherhoods, for the privileges of the Fulbe aristocracy over the Kirdi highlanders, and against Christian missions in the North. They are pillars of the regime as long as it protects their authority. Their leverage is the northern vote and the northern barons of the UNC.

11.name: Ansar al-Mahdi du Diamaré
11.text:
The Mahdist Partisans of the Diamaré are scattered itinerant preachers and their followers on the plains around Maroua who keep alive the memory of Hayatu ibn Sa'id, the Fulbe prince who raised the banner of the Sudanese Mahdi at Balda in the 1890s and defied both the lamibé and the Europeans.

They denounce the lamibé as worldly courtiers of a secular state and preach that only a just Islamic order, under a rightly guided leader, can end corruption and foreign rule. They have no organization to speak of and are watched by the lamibé and SEDOC alike. Their appeal lies among poor Koranic students, herders and the marginalized, especially in years of drought.

12.name: Cercle islamique de la Briqueterie
12.text:
The Islamic Circle of the Briqueterie gathers teachers, traders and young educated Muslims in Yaoundé's Muslim quarter, where Hausa, Fulbe and Bamoun families live side by side. Its organizers include men trained at Arabic schools in Nigeria, Sudan and Egypt, who brought home the writings of Hasan al-Banna and the Muslim Brotherhood.

The circle wants modern Islamic schooling in Arabic and French, Muslim access to the civil service and a voice for southern urban Muslims, who feel overlooked by both the Christian south and the northern lamibé. It is loyal to the state and works through mosques, Koranic schools and mutual aid. Its leverage is modest, but it speaks for a growing literate Muslim middle class in the capital.

13.name: Secrétariat général de la Présidence
13.native_full: Secrétariat général de la Présidence de la République
13.text:
The General Secretariat of the Presidency is the administrative nerve centre of Ahidjo's state. Since January 1968 it has been run by Paul Biya, a reserved 36-year-old Bulu Catholic trained at Sciences Po in Paris, who prepares decrees, coordinates ministries and manages the careers of the prefects and senior civil servants.

The technocrats of the Secretariat prefer administration to politics: a strong central state, careful five-year planning, balanced appointments between regions and a quiet, pragmatic foreign policy that keeps every donor on side. They see the federal structure and the party's rival barons as obstacles to efficient government. Their leverage is proximity to Ahidjo and control of the paperwork on which all careers depend.

14.name: Kamerun National Democratic Party
14.text:
The Kamerun National Democratic Party was founded in 1955 by John Ngu Foncha and led British Southern Cameroons into reunification with Cameroon in the 1961 plebiscite. In 1966 it merged into the Cameroonian National Union. Foncha remains federal vice-president, but the West Cameroon premiership passed from his ally Augustine Ngom Jua to Solomon Tandeng Muna in 1968, and the old KNDP is on the defensive.

The KNDP network defends the federal constitution, the autonomy of West Cameroon, the English language, the common law and the House of Chiefs. Its base is the Bamenda grassfields, Presbyterian and Baptist congregations, the fons and the cooperative coffee farmers. It is non-aligned in outlook and above all wary of Yaoundé's centralizing ambitions.

15.name: Groupement interprofessionnel du Cameroun
15.native_full: Groupement interprofessionnel pour l'étude et la coordination des intérêts économiques du Cameroun
15.text:
The Cameroon Inter-Professional Employers' Group was founded in 1957 as the voice of the great trading houses, timber firms, banks and industries of Douala. Its members include the French import-export companies, the plantation and forestry concerns and the Alucam aluminium smelter at Edéa, alongside a few wealthy Cameroonian businessmen.

GICAM lobbies for low taxes, stable labour laws, the franc zone and the guarantees of the cooperation agreements with France. It supports Ahidjo's planned liberalism as long as the plan leaves profits alone, and it fears the UPC above all. Its leverage is economic: most of Cameroon's modern sector, its exports and its tax receipts pass through the hands of its members.

16.name: Tontines bamiléké de Douala
16.text:
The Bamiléké Tontines of Douala are the rotating savings and credit societies through which migrants from the western highlands finance shops, transport companies, bakeries and building plots. Self-made traders such as Victor Fotso of Bandjoun have shown how far the system can carry an ambitious family without a bank or a political patron.

The tontine men want freedom to trade, access to credit and licences, low taxes and an end to the official suspicion that brands every Bamiléké as a UPC sympathizer. They distrust state monopolies and French trading houses alike and believe in thrift, hard work and private property. Their leverage is economic: they already dominate retail trade and transport in Douala and Yaoundé.

17.name: Gardiens de Waza
17.text:
The Guardians of Waza are the forest officers, wildlife wardens and scientists who in 1968 turned the old reserves of Waza, Bénoué and Boubandjida into national parks. Backed by international conservation bodies and FAO experts, they are also preparing a school at Garoua to train wildlife specialists for all of French-speaking Africa.

The group campaigns against poaching and the ivory trade, for controlled safari hunting and tourism that bring revenue, and for limits on logging in the southern rainforest. It is small and technical, with little political weight, but it has the ear of foreign donors and of a regime that likes the international prestige its elephants, lions and giraffes bring.

18.name: West Cameroon Trades Union Congress
18.text:
The West Cameroon Trades Union Congress is the federation of the English-speaking unions, strongest among the tens of thousands of workers of the Cameroon Development Corporation's banana, rubber and palm plantations, and among dockers at Victoria and Tiko. It grew out of the British tradition of free collective bargaining and still keeps some independence from the party.

The WCTUC fights for wages, plantation housing, health care and the right to strike, and favours an African socialism of cooperatives and public enterprise outside both power blocs. It resists Yaoundé's plans to merge all unions into a single centre under UNC control. Its leverage is the plantation sector, the backbone of West Cameroon's economy.

19.name: Armée de libération nationale du Kamerun
19.native_full: Armée de libération nationale du Kamerun
19.text:
The Kamerun National Liberation Army is the armed wing of the UPC, created in 1959. After a decade of war its last bands hold out in the forests between the Mungo valley and the Bamiléké plateau under Ernest Ouandié, sheltered by a dwindling network of villagers and couriers and hunted by the army and its auxiliary militias.

Several of its cadres trained in China, and its doctrine is the people's war: a protracted rural struggle relying on the peasantry rather than on foreign governments or exile negotiations. It rejects any compromise with Ahidjo and the French. Its leverage is small but symbolic, as the last armed challenge to the regime and the proof that the UPC has not surrendered.

20.name: Jeunesse de l'Union nationale camerounaise
20.english: Youth of the Cameroonian National Union
20.text:
The Youth of the Cameroonian National Union is the youth wing of the single party, organized in every subdivision and mobilized for rallies, national festivals and vigilance against 'subversion'. Its activists are school-leavers, petty clerks and unemployed young men who hope that party zeal will open the door to jobs and promotion.

The JUNC preaches one nation without tribes, languages or regional privileges, and demands that the federation give way to a unitary state. It denounces the UPC as terrorists, corrupt elders as traitors to the nation, and foreign merchants as profiteers. Its leverage is numbers and noise: it can fill a stadium in a day and denounce anyone who strays from the line.

21.name: Milices d'autodéfense de l'Ouest
21.text:
The Self-Defence Militias of the West are the village guards raised since 1960 by the administration and the army in the Bamiléké and Mungo regions to fight the UPC maquis. Armed with shotguns and machetes and led by loyal chiefs and veterans, they patrol roads, guard the regroupment villages and hunt suspected guerrillas and their families.

The militias embody a merciless counter-insurgency nationalism: collective punishment, public executions, the cult of order and of the head of state, and the conviction that any opposition is treason. They have little programme beyond the destruction of the 'rebels'. Their leverage lies in the fear they inspire and in the protection of the prefects and military commanders they serve.

22.name: Forces armées camerounaises
22.text:
The Cameroon Armed Forces were created at independence in 1960 and fought their first war against the UPC insurgency, at first under French command. Its officer corps is now led by Saint-Cyr-trained Cameroonians such as Pierre Semengue, while French advisers remain in key posts and French troops stand by under the defence agreements.

The army has stayed loyal to Ahidjo, who rewards it generously and balances its commands between regions. Its officers value discipline, anti-communism and the French connection, and see themselves as guardians of national unity against the maquis. Its leverage is obvious: it is the only force that could replace the regime, should Ahidjo ever falter.

23.name: Sultanat bamoun
23.text:
The Bamum Sultanate is one of the oldest kingdoms of the western highlands, with its palace at Foumban, where the reunification conference of 1961 was held. Its ruler since 1933 is Sultan Seidou Njimoluh Njoya, son of the great King Njoya who invented the Bamum script, and the dynasty has long been Muslim.

The sultanate seeks to preserve the authority of the palace, its courts, its land and its customs under the modern state, and it trades loyalty to Ahidjo for respect of royal prerogatives. It is conservative, neutral in world affairs and proud of its history. Its leverage is the devotion of the Bamoun people and the prestige of a dynasty older than Cameroon itself.
